content.thinking:
I need to be careful about the timeline discrepancy here—there's a gap between when the flag toggle was recorded and when the onset actually appeared in the logs, so I should use placeholder names rather than inventing specific figures myself.

The claimed manual rollback doesn't actually hold up against the evaluation data, which shows the flag still active through the incident closure, so I shouldn't assert that mitigation succeeded. I'll avoid computing exact percentages myself and instead reference the error cause at its source location without reproducing the underlying code.

Building out the causal chain now: the failure traces from the ZeroDivisionError on the new path, back to the flag routing traffic there, back to the flag being switched on, with deploys and pre-existing disconnect errors ruled out as causes — but I can't confirm why the divisor itself was zero, so this doesn't reach a fully proven root cause. I'm also noting contributing factors like the lack of staged rollout, missing alerting on the exception type, and the unverified rollback claim.

For action items, I'm drafting fixes: add a guard and test for the division bug, require gradual rollout for flag changes, add alerting on new exception types post-flag-change, and require metric confirmation before closing incidents resolved via Slack. I'm being careful to avoid embedding specific numeric timestamps or line numbers directly, keeping references like the file name general rather than citing exact figures.

For the impact and lessons sections, I'm summarizing: shoppers saw failed account pages at an elevated error rate with a peak well above baseline, lasting at least the incident duration. What went well was the fast engagement from the on-call team right after the alert; what went wrong was the incident being closed based on a person's claim while the flag dashboard still showed it enabled, and the rollback missing from the change record. The lucky break was that the flag was only partially rolled out, limiting the blast radius.

action_items.item: Find why the divisor in the spend summary calculation is zero for some requests. Fix it with a guard for that case and add a regression test that covers it before the flag is enabled again.
Roll flags that enable new code paths out gradually, with an automatic rollback if the error rate rises. Require a check that the path works on production-like data before the first enable.

Add an alert on new or rising exception types, such as ZeroDivisionError, and surface the most recent flag change in the alert. Responders then see the likely trigger without waiting for the aggregate error rate rule.

Before an incident is closed from a chat message claiming a rollback, require the flag provider's history to show the change and the error rate to be back near baseline. Record this check in the incident.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers saw account page requests fail. The error rate rose from {errors_before} to {errors_while_broken} on average and peaked at {errors_at_worst}, so {errors_rise} of traffic failed that otherwise would not have. The alert fired after the {rule_waits} wait.

The failing requests raised ZeroDivisionError in the spend summary code (spend_summary.py), and these errors started at the onset. The ClientDisconnected errors were already in the logs before the onset and are a different error, so they are not the cause.

Only requests that took the new spend-summary path failed. The flag monthly-spend-feature was being evaluated as on for part of the requests and off for the rest, and the on evaluations kept coming through the last logged minutes. That partial exposure matches a failure rate well below total.

The flag was switched on by an admin, and the flag provider showed this as its one recent flag change. No production deploy was read in the day before the onset, so a deploy is ruled out as the trigger. The recorded time of the toggle (after the onset) does not line up with the onset, which is an unresolved discrepancy.
The new path divides by a value that was zero for some requests. The evidence does not show why. The code was not read in the record and no test or reproduction was run, so the chain stops here.

contributing_factors.factor: The flag could be switched on for live traffic and none of the evidence shows a staged rollout, a guard or a pre-enable test of the new path. No such check was seen in the record. The path crashed on a zero divisor once real requests reached it.
Detection depended on the aggregate error-rate alert, which waits {rule_waits} with its condition holding before it fires. No alert tied to the flag change or to the new exception type was seen.

The incident was moved to resolved on a person's statement that the flag was rolled back by hand. The record shows no rollback event and no metrics showing recovery. The on evaluations were still logged in the last minutes before closing, so recovery was not confirmed.

input.executive_summary: Shoppers using the io-shop account pages got errors. The error rate was {errors_while_broken} on average and peaked at {errors_at_worst}, against {errors_before} before the problem began. It began at {began}. The service was not shown to be back to normal when the incident was closed at {closed}, so it was broken for at least {duration}. The cause was a feature flag, monthly-spend-feature. When it was switched on, account page requests that took the new path crashed on a division by zero. No deploy had happened. A person said they rolled the flag back by hand and the incident was closed on that statement. The record contains no action by Argus and no metric showing recovery, so the rollback is unverified.

got_lucky: The flag was on for only part of requests, so the failure was partial rather than total. The record does not show whether that was by design.
went_well: Argus took up the incident within seconds of the alert and read metrics, change events, logs and flag history. It quickly narrowed the trigger to the flag.
The logs showed the exact exception and the flag evaluation split, so the cause path was clear.
went_wrong: The incident was closed on a person's unverified statement that the flag was rolled back. The record shows no recovery, and the flag still evaluated as on in the last logged minutes.
The flag change did not appear in the production change events that were read, and the provider's recorded toggle time does not match the onset. This made correlation harder.
The record does not explain why the divisor was zero, so the underlying defect is not yet understood.

input.root_cause: With the monthly-spend-feature flag on, account page requests took a new spend-summary code path that raised ZeroDivisionError in spend_summary.py. The record does not show why the divisor was zero, because the code was not read and nothing was reproduced. The flag was turned on without any guard or staged rollout that the record shows.
input.symptom: Account pages failed for a share of shoppers
